item.title: PixelSmash – Critical FFmpeg Vulnerability Turns Media Files into Weapons
item.description:
CVE-2026-8461 (CVSS 8.8): heap OOB write in FFmpeg's MagicYUV decoder enables RCE via a single 50 KB media file upload, hitting Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Emby, Immich, OBS, and AI/ML pipelines.
- CVE-2026-8461 lives in libavcodec/magicyuv.c. When slice_height is odd (attacker-controlled via bitstream), ceiling-rounded chroma shifts accumulate an extra row per slice past the allocated buffer. With coded_height=32 and slice_height=31, the decoder writes 640 attacker-controlled bytes one full row beyond the Cb chroma plane, landing directly on the AVBuffer struct FFmpeg allocates immediately after pixel data.
- Exploitation overwrites AVBuffer.free with system() and AVBuffer.opaque with a shell command pointer. When av_frame_unref fires during normal frame cleanup, the hijacked indirect call executes the attacker's command before the process crashes. JFrog demonstrated a reverse shell on Jellyfin 10.9 (jellyfin-ffmpeg 7.1.3) via automatic library scan and on Nextcloud via the Movie preview provider, both triggered by uploading a single crafted AVI with zero authentication. ASLR was disabled for the RCE demo; without ASLR bypass the primitive reliably delivers DoS on every tested target.
- The torrent vector is zero-click: a malicious AVI dropped into Jellyfin's watched media folder triggers ffprobe automatically.

item.title: What Was a 45-GPU Cracking Farm Built For?
item.description:
A 45-GPU cracking farm turned raw FortiGate hashes into a validated, enriched access catalog of 74,000+ records across 22,000 orgs. Active credentials confirmed in sample testing, with an initial access broker already selling access.
- The operation was exposed by its own OPSEC failures: an open directory on port 9999 and a Hashtopolis panel on port 8443 running default credentials. Hashtopolis coordinated ~45 NVIDIA RTX 4090s across six agents with EPYC and Xeon Platinum hosts doing the heavy lifting, running hashcat at scale with rule-based and mask attacks. Last-activity timestamps align with first detected exploitation on 31 May 2026.
- Python tooling chained the full kill chain: LDAP recon pulling users, SPNs, and privilege flags; SMB/DFS crawlers hunting creds in config files; Kerberoasting and AS-REP targeting; then OSINT enrichment adding sector, revenue, and country to each record. Enrichment is the tell: you add revenue data when you plan to sell or rank.
- Forum user SantaAd posted ~34,000 FortiVPN entries on a Russian-language forum June 12, asking $60K opening bid, $120K blitz. C2 IPs include 185.229.26[.]83 and 213.169.49[.]142. Campaign favored management ports 443, 9443, 4443, 8443, and 10443.
If you run FortiGate, rotate all credentials now, pull management interfaces off the public internet, enforce MFA, and hunt for LDAP recon and Kerberoasting activity.

item.title: A VBScript campaign distributed through WhatsApp deploying RMM software
item.description:
Active WhatsApp campaign uses compromised accounts to push VBScript files that silently install ManageEngine Endpoint Central, giving attackers persistent RMM access. 80% of victims are in Malaysia 🇲🇾, with reach across Brazil 🇧🇷, India 🇮🇳, the UK 🇬🇧, and beyond.
- Compromised WhatsApp accounts send .vbs attachments with financial lure names ("Financial Reports.vbs", "Statement of Debt(30K).vbs") to the victim's contact list, no accompanying text. WScript.exe is spawned by WhatsApp.Root.exe from the AppData\Local\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions path, a reliable process-tree artifact. Stage 1 drops payloads into randomized C:\Users\Public\Documents\Temp_ or MSUpdate_ directories with hidden and system attributes set.
- Stage 2 modifies HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 0 via a looped ShellExecute runas call, silencing UAC prompts. A ZIP is then fetched using curl, bitsadmin, certutil, or PowerShell, extracted via Shell.Application CopyHere, and Zone.Identifier ADS stripped before setup1.vbs executes.
- Stage 3 silently installs a preconfigured ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent via msiexec.exe. The bundled DCAgentServerInfo.json points to attacker-controlled servers: 202.61.160[.]208, 202.61.160[.]201, 202.61.160[.]137, and 38.55.151[.]63.

item.title: Building a CI/CD pipeline for Sigma rules
item.description:
Detection as Code in practice: a full CI/CD pipeline for Sigma rules cuts out the "edit and save in the SIEM console" failure mode with automated validation, translation, testing, and shadow-mode deployment.
Key details:
- The four-stage pipeline is validate, translate, test, deploy. sigma-cli (wrapping pySigma) handles validation and conversion with no paid tooling. The SigmaHQ/sigma-rules-validator GitHub Action checks rules against the official JSON Schema. A 30-line Python script enforces metadata completeness: title, status, date, author, logsource, detection, and MITRE ATT&CK tags are all required or CI fails.
- Translated outputs (Sentinel KQL, Splunk SPL, Elastic Lucene) live under platform-translations/ as build artifacts generated by CI, never hand-edited. Field mapping pipelines applied at conversion time are where silent failures hide: a missing pipeline flag produces a syntactically valid query that matches nothing.
- Every rule needs two JSON fixtures: one true-positive event and one true-negative. pytest evaluates compiled queries against both. CERT-EU's droid goes further, running actual Atomic Red Team simulations in a sandbox and verifying the Sigma rule fires on real telemetry, eliminating "the fixture was wrong, not the rule" failures.
- New rules deploy to the SIEM with alerting suppressed for at least seven days (shadow mode). Match volume and event samples get human review before promotion.

item.title: Bypassing Microsoft Entra Conditional Access Policies via Nested App Authentication
item.description:
Microsoft Entra Conditional Access Policies could be fully bypassed via Nested App Authentication (NAA/BroCI), granting broad Microsoft Graph access even when CAPs were explicitly blocking a user. Patched June 2026.
Key findings:
- Three first-party app IDs bypassed CAP evaluation entirely when used as NAA targets against Microsoft Graph: ADIbizaUX (74658136-14ec-4630-ad9b-26e160ff0fc6), Intune for Education portal extension (f52f5287-0be2-4052-83e8-e69620aa67cc), and Intune portal extension (5926fc8e-304e-4f59-8bed-58ca97cc39a4). The Azure Portal app (c44b4083-3bb0-49c1-b47d-974e53cbdf3c) acted as the broker host.
- Attack chain: phish or AiTM to steal an Azure Portal refresh token, then use the NAA flow with brk_client_id and brk_redirect_uri parameters to mint a Graph token, completely skipping CAP. The ADIbizaUX app carries a massive pre-consented scope set and also exposes undocumented IAM APIs with no logging.
- The bypass window is bounded by a hard 24-hour SPA refresh token lifetime that cannot be extended, limiting but not eliminating the persistence opportunity.
Takeaway: Hunt your Entra sign-in logs for token requests to login.microsoftonline[.]com carrying brk_client_id targeting those three app IDs. Confirm the fix is in place by verifying AADSTS53003 is now returned for those flows. AiTM detections on Azure Portal authentication are your upstream control.

item.title: A Multi-Stage Steganographic Loader Campaign Deploying Diverse Payloads Globally
item.description:
A phishing campaign targeting India 🇮🇳 deploys Remcos RAT through a multi-stage steganographic loader chain, hiding payloads inside .NET Bitmap objects and executing entirely in memory to frustrate forensic recovery.
Key findings:
- Initial access via phishing archive dropping "GST Debit Note Apr_26.com", a packed unsigned 32-bit .NET executable masquerading as a brick game. The .com extension is deliberate misdirection. Filenames using NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, and GST themes confirm an India 🇮🇳-focused lure set.
- The loader extracts Optimax.dll from a serialized .NET Bitmap resource (SR1) using steganography, loads it via AppDomain.Load entirely in memory, which then reflectively loads "System Optimizer Ultimate.dll", which finally hollows Remcos into the user's default browser process. Nothing touches disk until persistence is set.
- Persistence hits three locations: a Run registry key in the Temp directory, winlogon.exe, and userinit. The malware also copies itself to AppData\Roaming under a randomized superhidden filename and bypasses UAC via eventviewer.exe.
- Remcos confirms itself with the mutex Remcos_Mutex_Inj, checks for sandboxes via sbiedll.dll and the registry key hardware/acpi/dsdt/vbox_, steals Chrome and Firefox credentials, logs keystrokes and window titles to logs.dat, and exfiltrates to 62.102.148[.]212:37393, 217.138.252[.]123:42830, and 146.70.244[.]90:37393.

item.title: Supercomputing on a Credit Card From The AI Rush Enabled The Massive FortiBleed Campaign
item.description:
The FortiBleed campaign exposed 75,000 Fortinet FortiGate firewalls by pairing commoditized infostealer credentials with rented GPU clusters, cracking hundreds of billions of hashes per second for roughly $14.40/hr.
Key details:
- Attackers rented 36 enterprise-class GPUs across six Vast.ai instances, managed via a Telegram bot running Hashtopolis. Against legacy Fortinet salted SHA-256 hashes, the cluster hit 720 billion hashes/second. Against modern PBKDF2, still 180-360 million/second. Valid credentials were then used to walk through the front door, no zero-day needed.
- Exported FortiOS config files were the primary harvest vector. Once cracked, attackers deployed network sniffers and captured roughly 143,000 Kerberos and 33,000 NetNTLM hashes targeting internal domain controllers, spanning 21,632 domains.
- The pipeline was fully AI-assisted: Cursor wrote management scripts and Telegram bots, open-source agentic pentest frameworks automated Active Directory enumeration post-pivot.
- Compromised FortiGates became supply chain beachheads, enabling lateral movement into MSPs, vendors, and trusted partners. Initial access was fueled by existing infostealer logs, not novel exploitation.
DFIR triage: audit logs for unexpected FortiOS config exports, cross-reference admin accounts against infostealer exposure databases, force credential rotation, and verify MFA is active and not dormant on all firewall admin accounts.

item.title: Inside the FortiBleed Open Directory: A Technical Analysis of What the Attacker Left Behind
item.description:
FortiBleed's open attacker server exposed the full credential-theft pipeline: harvesting, GPU cracking, and access sales, with CloudSEK separating verified compromises from inflated claims.
Key findings: - The open directory leaked the group's internal tooling and workflow, showing a structured operation: mass credential harvesting from Fortinet devices, offline GPU-accelerated password cracking, then monetization via access sales, not just data dumps - Verified compromises were a subset of what FortiBleed advertised, a critical distinction for defenders who may be triaging noise versus confirmed exposure - The attacker infrastructure itself became the artifact, directory listings, cracking configs, and harvested credential files giving researchers a rare inside view of the post-exploitation workflow - Access sales as the end goal means affected organizations face downstream risk beyond the initial Fortinet compromise: buyers may be unrelated threat actors pursuing ransomware or espionage objectives
DFIR takeaway: if your Fortinet estate has any exposure window in the relevant timeframe, treat credential reuse as a confirmed risk, not a hypothetical. Pull authentication logs for VPN and admin interfaces, hunt for logins from unusual ASNs or outside business hours, and force a credential rotation even if no alert fired.

item.title: Azure AD Graph Activity Logs: Ingestion and threat detection to close the visibility gap
item.description:
AzureADGraphActivityLogs finally close a decade-long visibility gap: ROADrecon, AADInternals, and FOCI token abuse against graph.windows.net were entirely invisible to SOCs until early 2026.
Key findings: - The legacy graph.windows.net surface (API versions 1.5, 1.6, 1.61-internal) went dark for defenders while offensive tooling like ROADrecon, AADInternals, and MSOLSpray hammered it freely. AzureADGraphActivityLogs only became available as a diagnostic category in early 2026, meaning years of directory enumeration produced zero capturable telemetry even with perfect logging configs. - Logs land in logs-azure.aadgraphactivitylogs-* with ECS fields including user_agent.original, source.ip, url.path, http.response.status_code, and azure.aadgraphactivitylogs.properties.api_version. The 1.61-internal version exposes strongAuthenticationDetail inline, a field Microsoft Graph gates behind a separate privileged endpoint, which is exactly why adversary tooling still targets the legacy API. - Five shipped detection rules cover the key recon shapes: suspicious user-agents (Python, aiohttp, curl, AzureHound), high 4xx ratios from a single caller, new (client, user) pairs indicating FOCI token swaps, unusual ASN origins, and an EQL sequence joining device-code sign-in to graph.windows.net enumeration within five minutes.

item.title: FortiBleed: Everything You Need to Know
item.description:
FortiBleed: 86,644 Fortinet devices compromised via credential stuffing and default passwords across 194 countries. No zero-day required. Operational security failure is the root cause.
Key findings: - The attack is a two-stage, self-reinforcing credential stuffing operation: attackers test known breach dump and infostealer credentials against internet-facing FortiGate and SSL VPN devices, then use compromised devices as passive network traffic sniffers to harvest additional credentials fed back into the scanner. Over 2,500 devices were breached with a single default credential (admin3:123456). - CVE-2026-24858, a FortiCloud SSO SAML authentication bypass (CVSS 9.8) disclosed January 2026, has been discussed as a possible contributor to initial access in a subset of cases, but is not the primary mechanism. This is not a zero-day campaign. - The stolen database is organized by country, sector, and organization revenue, the structure of an initial access inventory staged for sale. Telecom leads by volume; government, energy, healthcare, and financials are heavily represented. India 🇮🇳 and the US 🇺🇸 account for nearly a third of all entries. - Password rotation alone is insufficient. Attackers had admin access long enough to alter configs, add accounts, or adjust monitoring settings. Those changes survive a password reset.
Treat any device in the dataset as already compromised.

item.title: FortiBleed Campaign Exposing Credentials for 73,932 FortiGate Systems
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺-speaking threat group exposed valid admin and VPN credentials for 73,932 FortiGate firewalls across 194 countries, hitting government, critical infrastructure, NATO contractors, and finance with a GPU-cracking operation that leaves no login logs on victim devices.
Key findings: - Actors ran ~1.16 billion credential attempts against 320,777 FortiGate targets, intercepted SSL VPN auth hashes, then cracked them offline using a 45-GPU Hashtopolis cluster. Offline cracking means victim firewalls generated zero authentication log entries for the theft itself. - Insikt Group tied attacker infrastructure to 85[.]11[.]187[.]8 (AS211486). Artifacts recovered include fg_capture[.]log, ad_enum[.]py, spray_results[.]txt, backup_dfs[.]py, and log-clearing markers, confirming a full kill chain: capture, crack, AD enum, spray, exfil, cleanup. - A Turkish 🇹🇷 NATO defense contractor is among confirmed victims with classified documents allegedly exfiltrated, sharpening the espionage angle beyond opportunistic access. - Many affected devices were still online and internet-exposed at disclosure, running recent FortiOS versions, indicating no remediation had occurred.
Rotate all FortiGate admin and SSL VPN credentials now, enable MFA on every remote access path, and pull FortiOS logs for new admin accounts, config changes, and off-hours sessions. Then hunt inward: if those credentials touched AD, treat the domain as potentially enumerated.

item.title: MyBait: Why We Lured Attackers To Encrypt Our Cloud MySQL
item.description:
Exposed GCP CloudSQL with a weak root password was compromised twice in one day, both attackers dropped ransom notes within hours of brute-force success. AWS RDS and Azure MySQL were not breached under the same conditions.
Key findings: - GCP CloudSQL (root password "password", 0.0.0.0/0 access) was hit with brute-force within 8 minutes of deployment. Attacker one succeeded after 576 failed attempts, enumerated schema via SHOW DATABASES, SHOW TABLES, SHOW FIELDS, bulk-selected data with SELECT /\*!40001 SQL_NO_CACHE\*/, dropped tables, and created a RECOVER_YOUR_DATA ransom table demanding 0.0094 BTC to bc1qd9r8c0t7x0dw748f8ft5wng2wjf9puh29ay5ku. Contact: rambler+24hse@onionmail[.]org - Six hours later a second attacker found the first ransom note, locked it, and overwrote it with their own. Same day, same instance, two independent ransomware operators running automated campaigns. - The same attacker IP appeared in Postgres and MongoDB ransomware cases from separate research teams, confirming cross-database automated scanning and extortion at scale. - GCP requires explicit opt-in for data access logs and database audit flags (general_log, cloudsql_mysql_audit). Without those enabled, the query-level evidence trail does not exist by default.

item.title: Bleeding Out
item.description:
A well-resourced threat actor compromised 149+ Active Directory domains by using victim firewalls as passive PCAP sensors, harvesting 148,000+ Kerberos hashes and 33,000 NTLM hashes without touching internal endpoints.

A custom harvester extracts auth material from 15+ protocols including Kerberos pre-auth exchanges. No implants dropped on internal hosts, leaving a near-silent footprint. - AD exploitation follows with cracked creds: enumeration, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, delegation abuse, and file share staging. Confirmed exfiltration of classified defence documentation from a major defence electronics manufacturer elevates this beyond IAB or ransomware-precursor activity. - 7 Kali VMs auto-reinstall from cyberstrike[.]io on reboot. Decoy IPs are injected as false-flag attribution material and simultaneously act as canary validators in spray campaigns, deliberately corrupting IOC-based detection.

item.description:

item.title: DCOM Explained: How Attackers Turn a Windows Feature into a Lateral Movement Tool
item.description:
DCOM lateral movement exploits native Windows RPC infrastructure to execute commands remotely without dropping a single malicious file, making process-chain correlation your primary detection lever.
Key findings: - Attack chain (T1021.003): attacker dumps creds from lsass.exe on Machine A, authenticates to Machine B over TCP 135, instantiates MMC20.Application via CLSID C085698C-D16F-417A-8851-A263C70D21B6, then calls ExecuteShellCommand. No payload dropped; only signed Windows binaries touch disk. - Four-event correlation catches it: Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 (NTLM network logon) + Sysmon Event ID 3 (TCP 135 connection between workstations) + Sysmon Event ID 1 showing mmc.exe or excel.exe spawned under svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch + cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child of that DCOM host process. - The RPCSS Endpoint Mapper (rpcss.dll) handles port 135 negotiation and permission checks via HKCR\CLSID before SCM spawns the target process, so registry auditing on that key can surface unauthorized CLSID lookups. - Prevention: block TCP 135 between workstations at the firewall, strip remote activation rights from non-admin accounts in DCOM config, and deploy LAPS to break lateral reuse of local admin credentials.
Hunt for powershell.exe or cmd.exe whose grandparent is svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch. That two-hop parent chain is rare in legitimate traffic and is the clearest signal this technique leaves behind.

item.description:

item.title: Applying software engineering discipline to threat detection
item.description:
Treating detection rules as software artifacts eliminates the tribal-knowledge failures that let misconfigured SIEM rules fire 4,000 times overnight with no owner, no history, and no rollback path.
Key details: - Every detection rule belongs in Git with metadata: ATT&CK technique ID, data source, author, last reviewed date, and an explicit owner with an escalation path. Rules without ownership accumulate silently and become functionally dead while appearing active. - Sigma (YAML-based, vendor-neutral) compiles to Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL, Elastic EQL, Chronicle YARA-L, and more via sigma-cli/pySigma. The SigmaHQ repo gives you a maintained baseline to fork, not a blank page. Watch for field-name portability failures: a rule can compile cleanly and match nothing if target schema fields differ. - Every rule needs two test fixtures in CI: one malicious event it must match, one benign event it must not. Pull requests missing both should be rejected automatically, the same gate you apply to application code. - New rules enter shadow mode first (minimum 7 days, writes to a separate index, no analyst alert) before promotion. YARA-X adds a yr compile CI step for file/memory rules and clean JSON/YAML pipeline output.
Practitioner takeaway: start with five high-value rules, a Git repo, and a sigma-cli CI check that rejects PRs without test coverage.

item.title: FortiBleed — 75k Fortinet firewalls have admin passwords cracked
item.description:
75,000 Fortinet 🌐 firewall configs leaked with plaintext admin credentials, roughly 50% of all internet-facing FortiGate devices. Most are still online, most on recent patches, and the origin of the breach is unknown.
Key details: - Data confirmed legitimate by Hudson Rock. Includes full config exports with credentials visible only from the device itself. IP overlap with the 2025 Belsen Group leak (15k devices) is minimal, making this a largely separate, more recent compromise. - Fortinet moved to PBKDF2 credential storage in early-2025 firmware, but only re-hashes passwords after an admin logs in post-update. Devices patched but never re-authenticated still stored credentials as SHA-256 with salt, crackable offline. - The dataset is formatted with company name, revenue, and country, a standard eCrime initial-access broker format, suggesting this may be circulating for sale or already sold before publication. - In a majority of sampled devices the FortiGate management interface is exposed directly to the internet, giving any buyer of this data a direct login path to the firewall and the network behind it.
Takeaway: Rotate admin credentials on all FortiGate devices now, then force admins to log back in so PBKDF2 re-hashing triggers. Pull admin login logs and hunt for successful authentications you did not initiate. If you see unauthorized success events, treat the device as backdoored and replace it. item.title: Zombie COTables: Resurrecting Freed Memory to Escape VirtualBox
item.description:
A use-after-free in Oracle VirtualBox's SVGA subsystem enables guest-to-host escape with code execution in the hypervisor process. Patched in Oracle's January 2026 Critical Patch Update, the full exploit chain achieves ~70% reliability on Linux hosts.
Key technical details: - Root cause: `SVGA_3D_CMD_DESTROY_GB_MOB` frees a MOB (VMSVGAMOB, size 104 bytes) without checking if it is still bound to a Context-Object Table (COTable) via `aCOTMobs[]`, leaving a dangling pointer - Attack chain: bind MOB to COTable via `SVGA_3D_CMD_DX_SET_COTABLE` (type 7, SVGA_COTABLE_SAMPLER), destroy the MOB, reclaim freed heap chunks, force `RTMemAllocZ()` to place a new `VMSVGA3DDXCONTEXT` (0x2170 bytes) over the freed MOB buffer - Arbitrary write: `vmsvga3dDXDefineSamplerState()` uses guest-controlled `samplerId` as an unvalidated index into `cot.paSampler`, enabling out-of-bounds writes and pointer corruption - Info leak: heap grooming of 6 MOBs recovers base address of `VBoxDD.so` and `VMSVGAR3STATE` pointer, which contains exploitable function pointers (`pFuncsVGPU9->pfnCommandClear`) - ROP chain: stack pivot into guest-controlled command buffer, `RTMemProtect()` sets MOB buffer RWX, shellcode executes in hypervisor context. Process continuity preserved by redirecting execution back to `vmsvgaR3FifoLoop()`
Patch action: Apply Oracle January 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately.

item.title: Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk
item.description:
Dozens of malicious Wallpaper Engine packages discovered on Steam Workshop since late 2025, distributing DarkKomet backdoors, Lumma/Vidar infostealers, ransomware, and crypto miners. 89% of download attempts targeted gamers in China 🇨🇳, with Russia 🇷🇺 at 5.5%.
Key technical details: - Attack vector: "Application wallpaper" type in Wallpaper Engine executes arbitrary Windows binaries directly on the desktop - Sample infection chain: wallpaper drops `Synaptics.exe` (DarkKomet), launches `._cache_GAME1.exe` which side-loads a trojanized `AggregatorHost.dll` - Modified `AggregatorHost.dll` locates Steam credentials, hijacks the live session, and exfils to `hxxp://120.48.156[.]17/ey.php` - Second C2 cluster active at `hxxp://202.144.192[.]29` with staged payloads including `Themes2.zip` and `Synaptics.rar` via Dropbox - Malware families confirmed: DarkKomet (T1059), Lumma infostealer, Vidar infostealer, RenEngine loader, ransomware variants - Delivery variation: some packages used password-protected archives with the password embedded in the archive filename or a bundled JSON config file, enabling auto-extraction via script
Attribution note: diversity of tooling suggests multiple independent threat actors exploiting the same Steam Workshop upload mechanism rather than a single coordinated group. Compromised accounts were then abused to upload further malicious wallpapers, creating a self-sustaining distribution loop (T1608.001).
